events.title: Early Stone Age Inhabitants
events.description: Early humans in the Democratic Republic of the Congo region used stone tools, living by hunting and gathering. Archaeological evidence shows this area had rich natural resources and early human activities. These societies were small-scale, highly mobile, adapted to local environment.

events.title: Early Human Settlement
events.description: Archaeological evidence shows early human activity in the Congo Basin region. Hunter-gatherers settled in the dense tropical rainforests and river valleys. These early inhabitants developed tools and survival techniques adapted to the forest environment. The rich resources of the Congo River basin supported the development of human communities.

events.title: Neolithic Development
events.description: The Congo region entered the Neolithic period, with humans beginning to transition from pure hunting-gathering to early agricultural practices. Pottery-making techniques emerged, and people began domesticating plants such as yams and oil palms. Settlements along rivers increased, and population density rose. This period's technological advances laid the foundation for later social complexity.

events.title: Bantu Migration Begins
events.description: Bantu-speaking peoples began a massive migration from West Africa into Central and Southern Africa. This migration lasted thousands of years and fundamentally transformed the demographic landscape of the Congo region. The Bantu brought agricultural techniques, iron-working, and new forms of social organization. They gradually replaced or assimilated the indigenous Pygmy populations.

events.title: Agricultural Society Consolidation
events.description: Agricultural practices in the Congo Basin became more sophisticated, with people cultivating bananas, yams, and sorghum. Permanent villages were established, and social organization became more complex. Fishing became an important food source in river and lake regions. Population growth promoted the formation of trade networks.

events.title: Iron Age Arrival
events.description: The Congo region entered the Iron Age, with the introduction of iron-working technology revolutionizing agriculture, hunting, and warfare. Iron tools made forest clearing easier, facilitating agricultural expansion. Mastery of iron technology also promoted the formation of more complex social hierarchies and political organizations. Archaeological sites show advanced smelting techniques.

events.title: Early Trade Networks
events.description: Trade connections were established between different communities in the Congo region, exchanging salt, iron tools, pottery, and agricultural products. The Congo River and its tributaries became important transportation and trade routes. These early trade networks promoted cultural exchange and technology transfer, creating conditions for the later rise of kingdoms.

events.title: Early Kingdom Formation
events.description: Early political organizations and small kingdoms began emerging in the Congo region. These kingdoms were built on agricultural surplus, trade networks, and social stratification. Chiefs and kings began centralizing power and establishing tribute systems. This period laid the foundation for the rise of larger kingdoms later.

events.title: Rise of Luba Kingdom
events.description: In southeastern Congo, the Luba Kingdom began to form. Luba developed a sophisticated kingship system where kings were viewed as sacred rulers. Luba created a unique political system called 'bulupwe,' combining religious authority with secular power. Luba art and sculpture were renowned, and its political ideas influenced many surrounding kingdoms.

events.title: Kingdom of Kongo Established
events.description: The Kingdom of Kongo was founded by Nimi Lukeni, with its capital at Mbanza Kongo. This powerful kingdom controlled the lower Congo River region and developed a sophisticated administrative system, hierarchy, and trade networks. The Kongo Kingdom became one of the most powerful and organized states in Central Africa, with influence extending into present-day western DRC, Republic of Congo, Angola, and parts of Gabon.

events.title: Regional Trade Expansion
events.description: Trade networks between kingdoms and chiefdoms in the Congo region expanded. Copper, iron, salt, ivory, and raffia palm cloth became important trade commodities. Specialized artisan classes emerged, and towns developed as trade and craft centers. This period's economic prosperity supported the centralization of political power.

events.title: Portuguese Arrival
events.description: Portuguese explorer Diogo Cão reached the mouth of the Congo River, becoming the first European to contact the Kingdom of Kongo. This encounter opened diplomatic and trade relations between Kongo and Europe. The Portuguese were interested in Kongo's gold, ivory, and slaves. This marked a major turning point in Congolese history.

events.title: Christianization of Kongo
events.description: King Nzinga Nkuwu of Kongo and his court converted to Catholicism, with the king baptized as João I. Portuguese missionaries arrived in Kongo and began large-scale evangelization. Christianity merged with traditional beliefs, creating a unique Congolese Christianity. This religious transformation profoundly influenced Kongo's politics and culture.

events.title: Kongo Kingdom's Golden Age
events.description: The Kongo Kingdom reached its zenith in the 15th century, with an estimated population of 500,000. The capital Mbanza Kongo became a prosperous city with palaces, markets, and craft districts. The kingdom was divided into six provinces, each governed by a governor. Kongo developed a currency system using shell money called 'nzimbu.' The kingdom's administrative efficiency and organizational capacity were among the best in Africa at the time.

events.title: Reign of Afonso I
events.description: Afonso I (Afonso I Mvemba a Nzinga) became Kongo's most famous king. A devout Catholic, he attempted to modernize Kongo and establish equal relations with Portugal. He built schools and churches, and sent Kongolese nobles to study in Portugal. However, he strongly opposed the expansion of the slave trade, writing multiple letters to the Portuguese king in protest, but failed to stop the slave trade's destruction of Kongolese society.

events.title: Slave Trade Flourishes
events.description: The Atlantic slave trade expanded dramatically, with Kongo becoming a major source of slaves. Millions of Congolese were sold to plantations in the Americas. The slave trade led to continuous warfare, social upheaval, and population decline. The authority of the Kongo Kingdom gradually weakened as local lords warred with each other to obtain slaves. This period had a devastating impact on Congolese society.

events.title: Battle of Mbwila
events.description: The Kingdom of Kongo fought a decisive battle against Portugal at Mbwila. King António I was killed and the Kongolese army was defeated. This battle marked the end of the Kongo Kingdom as a unified power. Afterwards, Kongo descended into prolonged civil war and fragmentation, splitting into multiple hostile factions.

events.title: Kongolese Civil War Period
events.description: After the Battle of Mbwila, Kongo descended into decades of civil war. Multiple claimants fought for the throne, and the capital Mbanza Kongo was abandoned. This period is known as Kongo's 'Dark Age.' The slave trade continued to destroy social structures, and central authority almost completely collapsed.

events.title: Rise of Lunda Empire
events.description: In southeastern Congo, the Lunda Empire rose and expanded. The Lunda Kingdom controlled vast territories and established a complex tribute system. Lunda was known for its sophisticated political organization and trade networks, controlling copper, salt, and ivory trade. The Lunda Empire's influence extended into present-day DRC, Angola, and Zambia.

events.title: Rise of Tippu Tip
events.description: Zanzibar Arab-Swahili merchant Tippu Tip began building a commercial empire in eastern Congo. He controlled ivory and slave trade routes, establishing a quasi-state organization. Tippu Tip's sphere of influence covered large areas of eastern Congo. He allied with local rulers and became one of the most powerful figures in the region.

events.title: Kuba Kingdom Prosperity
events.description: The Kuba Kingdom in central Congo reached its zenith. Kuba was renowned for its refined art, textiles, and wood carvings. Kuba developed a complex political system and legal code. The Kuba Kingdom was relatively isolated and less directly affected by the slave trade, maintaining cultural and political stability.

events.title: British Exploration
events.description: British explorer James Kingston Tuckey led an expedition to explore the Congo River, attempting to find its source. Although the expedition failed due to disease, it marked increased European scientific interest in the Congo interior. The expedition's records inspired later exploration activities.

events.title: Arrival of Missionaries
events.description: European and American Christian missionaries began establishing mission stations in coastal and river regions of Congo. They built schools and clinics, attempting to spread Christianity and Western education. Missionary reports and letters increased European knowledge of Congo but also paved the way for colonialism.

events.title: Arab-Swahili Trade Expansion
events.description: Arab and Swahili merchants from East Africa extended their trade networks into eastern and central Congo. They established trading posts and controlled ivory and slave trade. These merchants brought Islamic influence and new trade goods but also intensified the slave trade in interior regions.

events.title: Stanley's Congo River Expedition
events.description: British-American explorer Henry Morton Stanley conducted an epic Congo River expedition, crossing from East Africa to the Atlantic. He mapped the Congo River and revealed the geography of the Congo Basin. Stanley's expedition reports generated enormous European interest in Congo, particularly from Belgian King Leopold II.

events.title: Leopold II's Ambitions
events.description: Belgian King Leopold II founded the International African Association, ostensibly for scientific and humanitarian purposes to explore Africa, but actually to build a personal colonial empire. Leopold hired Stanley to establish trading posts and sign treaties in Congo. This marked the beginning of Congo's colonization.

events.title: Stanley Works for Leopold
events.description: Stanley established a series of trading posts and administrative outposts in Congo on behalf of Leopold II. He signed treaties with hundreds of local chiefs, often deceptive, with chiefs not understanding they were surrendering sovereignty. Stanley built roads and infrastructure to the interior, laying the foundation for Leopold's colonial rule.

events.title: Berlin Conference
events.description: European powers convened in Berlin to partition Africa. Leopold II successfully lobbied nations to recognize his personal control over Congo. The conference recognized the Congo Free State as Leopold's private property, not a Belgian colony. This conference disregarded African peoples' rights and laid the legal foundation for colonial rule in Africa.

events.title: Congo Free State Established
events.description: The Congo Free State was officially established as Leopold II's private domain. This was a unique situation in history: a country becoming one person's private property. Leopold never visited Congo but implemented a brutal exploitation system through agents. The Congo Free State was about 76 times the size of Belgium.

events.title: Red Rubber Terror
events.description: Leopold II implemented a brutal rubber collection system. Congolese were forced to collect wild rubber, with those failing to meet quotas suffering torture, amputation, or execution. Villages were burned, hostages taken to force labor. An estimated 5 to 10 million Congolese died during this period, about half the population. This was one of the worst genocides in modern history.

events.title: Resistance Movements
events.description: Multiple uprisings against Leopold's rule erupted throughout Congo. The most famous included the Batetela rebellion and Arab-Swahili merchant resistance. These uprisings were brutally suppressed but showed Congolese people's determined resistance to colonial rule. Many traditional leaders led resistance movements.

events.title: Congo Reform Movement
events.description: British diplomat Roger Casement and American missionaries exposed the atrocities of the Congo Free State. Casement's report documented torture, amputations, and mass killings in detail. International public opinion was outraged, and the Congo Reform Association was founded to demand an end to Leopold's rule. Famous writers like Mark Twain and Arthur Conan Doyle joined the condemnation.

events.title: Belgium Takes Over Congo
events.description: Under international pressure, Leopold II was forced to transfer the Congo Free State to the Belgian government. Congo became Belgium's official colony, renamed Belgian Congo. Although the worst atrocities ended, colonial exploitation continued and Congolese still had no political rights.

events.title: Colonial Economic Development
events.description: Belgium developed mining in Congo, particularly copper, diamonds, and gold. Katanga Province became an important copper mining region. Belgium built railways, ports, and urban infrastructure, but mainly for resource extraction. Forced labor continued, and Congolese were excluded from economic benefits.

events.title: Simon Kimbangu Movement
events.description: Congolese religious leader Simon Kimbangu began preaching, founding the Kimbanguist sect. His teachings merged Christianity with African traditions, emphasizing African dignity and liberation. Belgian authorities viewed him as a threat, arrested Kimbangu, and sentenced him to life imprisonment. The Kimbanguist sect became an important spiritual force for Congolese nationalism.

events.title: Forced Cultivation System
events.description: The Belgian colonial government implemented a forced cultivation system, requiring Congolese farmers to grow cash crops such as cotton, coffee, and palm oil. Farmers were forced to abandon traditional food crop cultivation, leading to food shortages and famine. This policy caused widespread discontent, but resistance was brutally suppressed.

events.title: Accelerated Urbanization
events.description: Mining and colonial economic development led to large numbers of Congolese flooding into cities like Leopoldville (Kinshasa) and Elisabethville (Lubumbashi). Cities saw the emergence of a Congolese working class and small intellectual class. Racial segregation policies were strict, with Europeans and Congolese living in separate areas. Urbanization created a social basis for the later nationalist movement.

events.title: Colonial Education Expansion
events.description: Belgium expanded the education system in Congo, mainly operated by Catholic and Protestant missionary societies. Education focused on primary education and vocational training, with extremely limited higher education opportunities. The education system aimed to train obedient workers rather than independent thinkers. Nevertheless, these schools trained later nationalist leaders.

events.title: International Recognition of Congolese Art
events.description: Congolese traditional art, particularly sculpture and masks, began gaining recognition and acclaim in Europe. European artists like Picasso were inspired by African art. Ironically, many Congolese artworks were looted or purchased at low prices and placed in European museums. This sparked ongoing discussions about cultural heritage restitution that continue today.

events.title: Congo During WWII
events.description: During WWII, Belgian Congo supported the Allies, providing important strategic resources. Congo's uranium mines supplied raw materials for the US Manhattan Project, used to make atomic bombs dropped on Japan. Congolese soldiers fought in Africa and Burma. The war brought economic prosperity but also intensified Congolese desire for independence.

events.title: Development of Congolese Elite
events.description: After the war, a small group of educated Congolese (called 'évolués' or evolved ones) began to form. They were mostly civil servants, teachers, and clergy. Although they enjoyed slightly better status than ordinary Congolese, they still faced systemic discrimination. This group later became the core of the independence movement.

events.title: Congolese Economic Boom
events.description: In the early 1950s, Congo experienced an economic boom with record copper and diamond exports. Leopoldville and Elisabethville developed rapidly into modern cities. But economic benefits mainly flowed to Belgian companies and colonists, with Congolese workers receiving low wages and no political rights. Economic inequality intensified anti-colonial sentiment.

events.title: Van Bilsen Plan
events.description: Belgian Colonial Minister Van Bilsen proposed a thirty-year independence plan, suggesting Congo gradually achieve independence over 30 years. This moderate proposal was viewed as radical in Belgium but considered too slow in Congo. This showed the huge divergence between colonizers and colonized on independence timelines.

events.title: Kinshasa Manifesto
events.description: Congolese intellectuals published the 'Conscience Africaine' manifesto, demanding gradual independence and political reform. This was an important milestone in the Congolese nationalist movement. The manifesto called for ending racial discrimination and giving Congolese more political rights. This marked the public emergence of the Congolese independence movement.

events.title: ABAKO Manifesto
events.description: Katanga intellectuals published the ABAKO Manifesto, led by Joseph Kasavubu. The manifesto demanded immediate independence, opposing Van Bilsen's gradual plan. The ABAKO organization represented Bakongo interests, emphasizing ethnic identity. This marked the rise of radical nationalism.

events.title: First Municipal Elections
events.description: Belgium allowed Congolese to participate in limited municipal elections. This was the first time Congolese gained voting rights, though power was very limited. Elections sparked political activity, with multiple parties forming. These elections laid the foundation for the later independence movement.

events.title: Lumumba's Rise
events.description: Patrice Lumumba became leader of the Congolese National Movement (MNC). Lumumba was a radical pan-Africanist demanding immediate independence and African unity. His charisma and oratory made him Congo's most popular political leader. Lumumba represented Congolese people's desire for true independence and dignity.

events.title: Leopoldville Riots
events.description: Massive riots erupted in Kinshasa (then Leopoldville) protesting colonial rule and racial discrimination. Belgian troops suppressed the riots, killing dozens. The riots shocked the Belgian government, making it realize it must accelerate decolonization. These riots accelerated Congo's path to independence.

events.title: Mobutu's Coup
events.description: Army Colonel Joseph-Désiré Mobutu (later renamed Mobutu Sese Seko) staged a coup, neutralizing Lumumba and Kasavubu. Mobutu had CIA support, as the US feared Lumumba's leftist leanings. Mobutu established a technocratic government but actually held military power. This was the beginning of Mobutu's 32-year rule.

events.title: Congo Independence
events.description: The Democratic Republic of the Congo (then called Republic of the Congo) declared independence, ending 75 years of colonial rule. Lumumba delivered a famous speech at the independence ceremony, condemning colonial atrocities and calling for true independence and dignity. His speech angered Belgian King Baudouin but won enthusiastic support from Congolese people. Independence Day was full of hope but also foreshadowed the coming crisis.

events.title: Brussels Round Table Conference
events.description: The Belgian government and Congolese political leaders held a round table conference in Brussels to discuss independence. The conference decided Congo would become independent on June 30, 1960. This timeline was very rushed, with Congo lacking administrative personnel and infrastructure prepared for independence. Belgium's sudden withdrawal set the stage for later chaos.

events.title: Pre-Independence Elections
events.description: Congo held its first national elections. Lumumba's Congolese National Movement won the most seats but not an absolute majority. Election results reflected Congo's regional and ethnic divisions. Lumumba was appointed Prime Minister, Joseph Kasavubu as President. Political divisions threatened national unity from the start.

events.title: Army Mutiny and Katanga Secession
events.description: Just one week after independence, the Congolese army (Force Publique) mutinied, protesting continued Belgian officer rule and low wages. Violence and chaos spread nationwide. Belgium sent troops without permission to protect expatriates. Katanga Province declared independence under Moïse Tshombe, supported by Belgian mining companies. Congo descended into crisis.

events.title: UN Intervention
events.description: Lumumba requested UN assistance to restore order and expel Belgian troops. The UN sent peacekeeping forces (ONUC) into Congo. But the UN refused to help Lumumba reunify Katanga, disappointing Lumumba. Lumumba turned to the Soviet Union for aid, which alarmed Western countries in the Cold War context.

events.title: Lumumba's Arrest and Murder
events.description: Lumumba attempted to reach Stanleyville (Kisangani) to establish a new government but was arrested en route by Mobutu's troops. On January 17, 1961, Lumumba was transferred to Katanga and executed by Tshombe's forces with Belgian and American complicity. Lumumba's murder is one of the most controversial events in Congolese history. He became a martyr and symbol of the African independence movement.

events.title: Congo Crisis Continues
events.description: After Lumumba's death, Congo descended into civil war and fragmentation. Multiple regions declared independence or autonomy, including Katanga, South Kasai, and Kivu. UN peacekeepers tried to restore order. Lumumba's supporters established a rival government in Stanleyville. This period was filled with violence, political assassinations, and foreign intervention.

events.title: End of Katanga Secession
events.description: Under UN military action and international pressure, Katanga's secession movement was crushed. Tshombe fled into exile. Katanga was reintegrated into Congo, but the province's mineral wealth continued to be a focus of political struggle. The end of the Katanga crisis marked the end of the most severe phase of the Congo Crisis, but the country remained unstable.

events.title: Simba Rebellion
events.description: Lumumba's supporters launched a large-scale rebellion called the Simba Rebellion. Rebels controlled large areas of eastern Congo, including Stanleyville. The rebellion had Soviet and Chinese support. Government forces counterattacked with Belgian, American, and mercenary assistance. The rebellion was accompanied by massive violence and atrocities, with thousands killed.

events.title: Mobutu's Second Coup
events.description: Mobutu staged another coup, this time permanently seizing power and overthrowing President Kasavubu. Mobutu claimed to end political chaos and build a strong central government. He established dictatorial rule and banned all opposition parties. Mobutu's rule would last 32 years, becoming one of Africa's longest and most autocratic dictatorships.

events.title: One-Party State Established
events.description: Mobutu established a one-party state, creating the Popular Movement of the Revolution (MPR) as the only legal party. All Congolese citizens automatically became party members. Mobutu centralized all power, controlling government, military, and economy. Opposition was suppressed, political dissidents imprisoned or exiled. This marked the end of Congolese democracy and consolidation of personal dictatorship.

events.title: Authenticity Campaign
events.description: Mobutu launched the 'Authenticité' campaign, aimed at restoring African cultural identity and rejecting colonial heritage. The Republic of Congo was renamed Zaire, Leopoldville became Kinshasa, Stanleyville became Kisangani. Citizens were required to abandon Christian names and adopt African names. Mobutu himself changed his name to Mobutu Sese Seko Kuku Ngbendu Wa Za Banga.

events.title: Zairianization Policy
events.description: Mobutu implemented 'Zairianization' policy, nationalizing foreign-owned businesses and plantations, then distributing them to his cronies. This policy was nominally economic nationalism but actually massive plunder and corruption. Many businesses were mismanaged, productivity declined. Zairianization destroyed Congo's economy but made Mobutu and his cronies extremely wealthy.

events.title: Ali-Foreman Boxing Match
events.description: Mobutu hosted the Muhammad Ali vs. George Foreman world heavyweight boxing championship in Kinshasa, called the 'Rumble in the Jungle.' The match attracted global attention, and Mobutu used it to enhance Zaire's international image and his personal prestige. The match was extremely expensive while Zairian people lived in poverty.

events.title: Intervention in Angolan Civil War
events.description: Zaire intervened in the Angolan Civil War, supporting opposition organizations FNLA and UNITA against the Soviet and Cuban-backed MPLA government. Mobutu feared Angola's communist government would threaten his rule. Zaire had US and South African support. This intervention exacerbated regional instability and consumed vast Zairian resources.

events.title: Shaba Wars
events.description: Exiled Katangese gendarmes invaded Zaire's Shaba Province (former Katanga) from Angola, attempting to overthrow Mobutu. Zairian forces were unable to resist, and France and Morocco sent troops to assist Mobutu. These two invasions (called Shaba War I and II) exposed the weakness of Zairian forces and Mobutu's dependence on foreign support.

events.title: Economic Collapse
events.description: Zaire's economy deteriorated sharply in the 1980s. Copper prices fell, corruption was rampant, infrastructure collapsed. Hyperinflation destroyed currency value. Wages couldn't be paid, public services stopped functioning. Roads, bridges, and railways fell into disrepair. Zaire transformed from a potentially wealthy country into a typical example of a failed state. Mobutu and his cronies accumulated billions of dollars in wealth.

events.title: Multi-Party System Announced
events.description: Under domestic pressure and reduced Western support after the Cold War ended, Mobutu announced the end of one-party rule and allowed multi-party democracy. This marked the beginning of loosening Mobutu's dictatorship. But Mobutu tried to manipulate the democratization process to maintain power. Opposition organized and demanded real reform.

events.title: Army Riots and Looting
events.description: Unpaid Zairian troops rioted in Kinshasa and other cities, engaging in massive looting and destruction. Hundreds died, the economy further collapsed. France and Belgium sent troops to evacuate expatriates. These riots showed the complete collapse of Mobutu's regime and the disintegration of state institutions.

events.title: Chaotic Transition Period
events.description: Zaire entered a long and chaotic political transition. Power struggles between Mobutu and opposition continued. A national conference convened but couldn't reach consensus. The economy continued deteriorating, violence and anarchy spread. Mobutu's health declined, he frequently traveled to Europe for cancer treatment. The state was effectively in collapse.

events.title: Impact of Rwandan Genocide
events.description: After the Rwandan genocide, about 2 million Hutu refugees (including militias who participated in the genocide) fled into eastern Zaire. Refugee camps became bases for Hutu extremists who attacked Rwanda from there. This completely changed Great Lakes region geopolitics and set the stage for later Congo wars. Mobutu's allowing genocidaires to shelter in Zaire angered Rwanda's new government.

events.title: First Congo War Begins
events.description: Rwanda and Uganda-backed rebels launched an insurgency under Laurent-Désiré Kabila, aiming to overthrow Mobutu. The Alliance of Democratic Forces for the Liberation of Congo-Zaire (AFDL) advanced rapidly, gaining local popular support. Mobutu's forces collapsed with almost no resistance. This war was also called 'Africa's First World War.'

events.title: Mobutu's Fall and Kabila's Rise
events.description: Kabila's rebels entered Kinshasa, Mobutu fled to Morocco. Mobutu's 32-year dictatorship ended. Kabila declared himself president and renamed the country Democratic Republic of the Congo. Mobutu died in Morocco in September that year. Kabila promised democracy and reconstruction but quickly showed autocratic tendencies.

events.title: Second Congo War Begins
events.description: Kabila broke with former allies Rwanda and Uganda, who supported a new rebellion. Congo descended into war again, this time on a larger scale involving nine African countries and dozens of armed groups. Angola, Zimbabwe, and Namibia supported Kabila's government. This war was called 'Africa's World War' or 'the Great War,' becoming one of the deadliest conflicts since WWII.

events.title: Great War and Humanitarian Disaster
events.description: The Second Congo War caused about 5.4 million deaths, most from disease and starvation rather than direct combat. The war was accompanied by massive sexual violence, child soldier recruitment, and civilian massacres. Eastern Congo became anarchic, with dozens of armed groups fighting for territory and resources. Illegal mining of mineral resources (especially cobalt, diamonds, and coltan) financed the war. This was one of the worst humanitarian disasters in modern history.

events.title: Kabila Assassinated
events.description: Laurent-Désiré Kabila was assassinated in the presidential palace by his bodyguard Rashidi Kasereka. The assassination's motive and mastermind remain unclear. Kabila's son Joseph Kabila was quickly appointed president at age 29. The rapid power transition avoided greater chaos but raised questions about legitimacy.

events.title: Peace Negotiations
events.description: Under international pressure, the Congolese government, rebels, and foreign armies began peace negotiations. South Africa hosted the Sun City talks. Parties agreed to a power-sharing agreement and foreign troop withdrawal. But the peace process was fragile, violence continued in the east.

events.title: Transitional Government Formed
events.description: According to the peace agreement, an inclusive transitional government was formed with Joseph Kabila as president and four vice presidents representing different factions. This '1+4' government aimed to pave the way for elections. Foreign armies officially withdrew, but many armed groups remained active. UN peacekeeping forces (MONUC) expanded, becoming the UN's largest peacekeeping operation.

events.title: First Democratic Elections
events.description: Congo held its first free elections in over 40 years. Joseph Kabila won the presidency in a second-round vote against Jean-Pierre Bemba. Elections were deemed generally free and fair by international observers, despite some problems. This marked an important step in Congo's democratization but also exposed deep regional and ethnic divisions.

events.title: Kivu Conflict Escalates
events.description: Conflict in eastern Congo's North Kivu Province escalated, with Tutsi rebel leader Laurent Nkunda's forces battling government troops. Hundreds of thousands of civilians were displaced. Nkunda claimed to protect Tutsis from Hutu militia attacks. The conflict's roots lay in the legacy of the 1994 Rwandan genocide, land disputes, and mineral resource control.

events.title: Nkunda Arrested and CNDP Integration
events.description: After Rwanda and Congo reached an agreement, Nkunda was arrested in Rwanda (where he remains under house arrest). His rebel organization CNDP integrated with Congolese forces. But many CNDP members were dissatisfied with integration terms and continued fighting or joined new armed groups. Peace in the east remained elusive.

events.title: Controversial Elections
events.description: Joseph Kabila won re-election in highly controversial elections. Opposition leader Étienne Tshisekedi claimed the election was rigged and refused to accept the results. International observers reported serious irregularities. Post-election violence killed dozens. These elections damaged Kabila's legitimacy and intensified political tensions.

events.title: M23 Rebellion
events.description: Former CNDP members formed a new rebel organization M23 (March 23 Movement), named after the date of the 2009 peace agreement. M23, supported by Rwanda, quickly captured large areas of North Kivu Province, including the important city of Goma. UN reports confirmed Rwandan and Ugandan support for M23. The international community condemned foreign intervention.

events.title: M23 Defeated
events.description: With support from the UN Intervention Brigade (FIB), Congolese forces defeated M23 rebels. This was the first time UN peacekeepers received an offensive combat mandate. M23 leaders fled to Rwanda and Uganda. M23's defeat was a major victory for the Congolese government, but dozens of other armed groups remained active in the east.

events.title: Third Term Crisis
events.description: Kabila's second and constitutionally final term was set to end in 2016, but he refused to commit to stepping down. The government postponed elections, triggering massive protests. Security forces violently suppressed demonstrations, killing dozens. Opposition and civil society demanded respect for the constitution and Kabila's departure. Congo descended into a serious constitutional crisis.

events.title: Christmas Massacre
events.description: Security forces violently suppressed peaceful protests organized by the Catholic Church in Kinshasa, killing dozens. The Church became an important voice against Kabila, demanding elections. The crackdown drew international condemnation, but Kabila continued refusing to step down.

events.title: Kasai Conflict
events.description: Serious ethnic violence erupted in Kasai-Central Province, with conflict between government forces and traditional militia Kamuina Nsapu causing thousands of deaths and displacing 1.4 million people. The conflict originated from the government killing a traditional chief, but roots lay in political marginalization and economic grievances. This was one of Congo's worst humanitarian crises in recent years.

events.title: Presidential Elections
events.description: After multiple postponements, Congo finally held presidential elections. Kabila didn't run, supporting his former Interior Minister Emmanuel Ramazani Shadary. Opposition was divided, with main candidates Félix Tshisekedi and Martin Fayulu. The electoral process was controversial, including voting machine failures and election cancellations in some areas.

events.title: Tshisekedi Elected President
events.description: The electoral commission declared Félix Tshisekedi the winner, making him Congo's new president. This was Congo's first peaceful power transfer in history. But Catholic Church election observers and many analysts believed Fayulu was the real winner, suspecting Kabila and Tshisekedi reached a power-sharing deal. Despite controversy, Tshisekedi's inauguration marked the end of the Kabila era.

events.title: Tshisekedi-Kabila Power Struggle
events.description: Power struggles between President Tshisekedi and former President Kabila dominated politics. Kabila's FCC party controlled a parliamentary majority, limiting Tshisekedi's power. Tshisekedi tried to escape Kabila's influence by appointing his own prime minister and cabinet. This 'cohabitation' arrangement caused political deadlock and governance difficulties.

events.title: Ebola Outbreak
events.description: Eastern Congo experienced the second-worst Ebola outbreak in history, causing over 2,000 deaths. The outbreak occurred in North Kivu and Ituri provinces, with ongoing conflict and community distrust hindering response efforts. Health workers were attacked, treatment centers burned. The international community provided aid, new vaccines were used. The outbreak was declared over in June 2020, but new cases emerged months later.

events.title: Coalition Breakup
events.description: Tshisekedi officially ended his alliance with Kabila's FCC, forming a new parliamentary majority. This was a major move by Tshisekedi to consolidate power. He appointed a new prime minister and cabinet, more composed of his allies. This marked a significant decline in Kabila's political influence but also raised questions about democratic procedures.

events.title: Eastern Violence Escalates
events.description: Violence in eastern Congo escalated sharply, particularly in Ituri and North Kivu provinces. Multiple armed groups including ADF (Allied Democratic Forces, linked to Islamic State), CODECO, and other militias conducted massacres and attacks. Thousands of civilians were killed, hundreds of thousands displaced. The government declared a state of siege, but violence continued. The humanitarian crisis worsened, with millions needing aid.

events.title: Nyiragongo Volcano Eruption
events.description: Mount Nyiragongo erupted near Goma, with lava flows destroying hundreds of homes and forcing hundreds of thousands to flee. This was the most serious eruption since 2002. Although central Goma was spared, suburbs suffered severe damage. Volcanic activity continued for weeks, raising fears of a larger eruption. This disaster highlighted eastern Congo's vulnerability and inadequate response capacity.

events.title: M23 Resurgence
events.description: M23 rebels became active again after years of dormancy, launching offensives in North Kivu Province. M23 quickly captured large territories, approaching Goma. The UN and Congolese government accused Rwanda of again supporting M23, which Rwanda denied. Hundreds of thousands were displaced again. The East African Community (EAC) deployed regional forces to try to stabilize the situation. M23's resurgence set back the eastern peace process.

events.title: M23 Crisis Continues
events.description: M23 continued advancing in North Kivu Province, capturing strategic towns like Rutshuru and Kiwanja. Congo-Rwanda relations deteriorated sharply, with both countries on the brink of war. Millions were displaced, the humanitarian crisis intensified. International mediation efforts had limited success. M23's offensive triggered anti-Rwandan sentiment and violence against Tutsi civilians.

events.title: 2023 Elections
events.description: Congo held presidential, parliamentary, and local elections. Félix Tshisekedi sought re-election, facing multiple challengers including Moïse Katumbi, Martin Fayulu, and Matieu Madalou. The electoral process was chaotic, with many polling stations opening late and technical problems widespread. Opposition alleged massive fraud. Despite controversy, Tshisekedi declared victory.

events.title: Tshisekedi's Second Term
events.description: Félix Tshisekedi began his second presidential term, promising to address security, economic, and governance issues. But Congo faces enormous challenges: ongoing conflict in the east and M23 threat, economic difficulties, corruption, infrastructure collapse, and humanitarian crisis. Millions are displaced and need humanitarian aid. Congo has rich mineral resources (cobalt, copper, diamonds, gold, coltan), but most of the population lives in extreme poverty. Illegal mining and resource smuggling finance armed groups. Congo's future depends on achieving peace in the east, improving governance, fighting corruption, and converting mineral wealth into people's welfare. Congo's stability is crucial for the entire Great Lakes region and Central Africa. As Africa's second-largest country and fourth most populous (about 100 million people), Congo's potential is enormous, but realizing this potential requires overcoming decades of conflict, exploitation, and misgovernance legacy.
